What clay shooting is

Clay shooting is a sport in which a shooter breaks small flying discs with a shotgun. The disc is called a target or a clay; shooters often call it a bird, but nobody shoots at live animals. The FITASC rules say plainly that shooting at live animals is not allowed, and safety and care for the environment come first.

A machine called a trap throws each target. Its path through the air (or along the ground) is the trajectory. The gun is a shotgun with smooth barrels (smooth-bore: no spiral grooves inside, unlike a rifle). It fires a cartridge full of small pellets called shot, which spread into a small cloud. That is why the shooter points the gun where the target is going, not where it is now.

A trap spins the target and throws it at a set speed and angle. Trajectories vary a lot: a target may come towards you, go away, cross in front of you, fly high or roll along the ground.

This course is about two disciplines (two kinds of clay shooting) of the international federation FITASC. Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ (Sporting™ for short) imitates hunting. Its traps are often hidden or screened by bushes and trees, and targets fly like a partridge, a duck or a pheasant, or roll like a hare. Compak® Sporting is the compact version: the same variety of targets, but on one small field with five stations in a line and six traps.

You will also hear about Trap and Skeet. They are different disciplines with set trajectories. In Skeet the trajectories are always the same; in Trap the targets fly at changing angles from a fixed set, in an order the shooter does not know. Olympic Trap and Skeet belong to another federation. Do not mix their rules with Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting.

A hit is visible at once: the target breaks or at least a visible piece flies off. This clarity is what makes the sport easy to watch and, for you, easy to follow from the very first day.

The sport grew out of hunting. Shooters once practised on live birds; from the late 1800s clay targets began to take their place. Today clay shooting is a sport of its own, with rules, referees and international competitions. More history: From live birds to clay targets.

You can shoot just for fun or compete. Many people come to a shooting ground to spend a day outdoors with friends; some later enter club shoots and championships. The disciplines are compared in The main disciplines.

Key points

  • People shoot at clay targets thrown by traps, never at live animals.
  • A shotgun fires a cloud of small pellets (shot), so the shooter points ahead of the target.
  • Sporting™ imitates hunting over natural ground; Compak® Sporting is its compact version on one field.
  • Trap and Skeet are other disciplines with their own rules.
  • A hit is visible at once: the target breaks or a visible piece flies off.

Did you know?

Targets are made brittle on purpose, so even a few pellets can break them.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Watch this bird off trap B.

    Meaning: 'Bird' is a target, not a real bird; trap B is the machine marked B.

  • Coach Today we walk the Sporting course, tomorrow it's Compak.

    Meaning: Two different disciplines on two different days.

  • Coach Point it, don't aim it.

    Meaning: A shotgun is swung and pointed with both eyes on the target, not aimed like a rifle.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. A coach says 'Watch the next bird.' What will you see?

    1. A live pigeon released from a box
    2. A clay target thrown by a trap
    3. A bird-shaped paper target on a board
    4. A drone
    Answer

    A clay target thrown by a trap

    'Bird' is shooters' slang for a clay target; the FITASC rules forbid shooting at live animals.

  2. What does a shotgun fire?

    1. One single bullet
    2. A small arrow-like dart
    3. A cloud of small pellets (shot)
    4. A ball filled with paint
    Answer

    A cloud of small pellets (shot)

    The shot leaves the muzzle as a small cloud of pellets, so the shooter points ahead of the moving target.

  3. Which statement about Compak® Sporting is correct?

    1. A compact version on one field, stations in a line
    2. It is the Olympic version of the Skeet discipline
    3. It is shot only at live game birds in the field
    4. It uses a single trap and a single station
    Answer

    A compact version on one field, stations in a line

    Compak® Sporting brings Sporting™-style targets onto one small field with five stations and six traps.
